title: The Master Sommelier Diploma
lead: What the Court's highest title asks of you: who can apply, the three parts and the 75% mark, how the oral theory works, the practical and six-wine tasting, and the clock that starts when you pass Theory.

intro.title: THREE PARTS, 75% EACH
intro.text: The Master Sommelier Diploma has the same three parts as the Advanced exam. The pass mark on each part rises from 60% to 75%.

lines.label: The title
lines.text: The Court calls Master Sommelier the highest honor in the field: mastery of wine knowledge, hospitality and service, deductive tasting and business.

lines.label: The way in
lines.text: Only those who have passed the Advanced Sommelier exam may apply. The Introductory, Certified and Advanced levels all come first.

know: Passing the Advanced Sommelier Examination makes you eligible to apply for the Master Sommelier Diploma.
You apply with the Court's Application of Intent. An email saying you intend to sit is not accepted.
There are two applications: Theory (first-timers and anyone who has reset) and Practical and Tasting (anyone holding at least Theory).
The examiners are Master Sommeliers chosen by the Examination Committee under the Court's Examiner Rotation Policy.
The Court's About page says the road often takes 5 to 10 years, or longer.

lines.label: The parts
lines.text: An oral theory exam, a practical exam in wine service and business, and a deductive tasting of six wines.

lines.label: The bar
lines.text: Each part needs at least 75%. At Advanced the mark was 60%.

know: The theory exam is oral, not written.
The practical covers restaurant wine service and salesmanship; the Court's About page adds business calculations.
The Court's practical feedback example reports on a Sparkling table, a Decanting table and Business of the Sommelier.
The tasting is six wines in 25 minutes; the Court's About page says three whites and three reds.
Candidates wear professional working attire and bring every tool of the sommelier trade.

facts.fact: The Master Sommelier title is the highest honor in the field, representing mastery of wine knowledge, hospitality and service, deductive tasting and business fundamentals.
Students who pass the Advanced Sommelier Examination are eligible to apply for the Master Sommelier Diploma Examination.

Before the Master Sommelier Diploma, candidates go through three mandatory prerequisite levels: Introductory Sommelier Course & Examination, Certified Sommelier Examination, Advanced Sommelier Course & Examination.
Becoming a Master Sommelier typically takes several years; on average 5 to 10 years or longer (About page).
Candidates must complete the Application of Intent; emails stating intent are not accepted.
Theory application: for those sitting the first time or who have reset and hold no portions. Hospitality & Service Practical and Tasting application: for those holding at least the Theory portion.
Members of the examining panel are Master Sommeliers chosen by the Examination Committee according to the CMS-A Examiner Rotation Policy.
The exam has three parts like the Advanced: a theory examination (oral, not written), a deductive tasting of six wines, and a practical wine service and business examination.
Minimum passing score on each of the three sections is 75%, as opposed to 60% for the Advanced Sommelier Examination.

Candidates wear professional working attire, provide all tools of the sommelier trade, show the highest technical skill and knowledge, the courtesy and hospitality of a Master Sommelier, and excellent salesmanship (described as essential).

Practical: aperitifs; glassware for all beverages in lounge, restaurant or private function room; menu and wine list recommendations with vintages; present, prepare (decanting when necessary) and serve wines; brandies, liqueurs and spirits with proper portions; questions and complaints with skill, elegance and diplomacy.

The About page describes the Hospitality & Service portion as a restaurant-like scenario including presentation, decanting, glassware selection, pairing recommendations, business calculations and salesmanship.
The MS Practical feedback reports on the Sparkling Table, Decanting Table and Business of the Sommelier; Tasting feedback reports Sight, Nose & Palate, Structure and Conclusions.

Tasting: candidates describe six different wines clearly and accurately within twenty-five minutes, identifying where appropriate grape varieties, country, district and appellation of origin, and vintages.
The About page describes the tasting as 6 wines tasted blind in 25 minutes, 3 red and 3 white, done verbally before a panel of Master Sommeliers.
The About page describes the Theory as a one-hour verbal exam that also covers beer, sake, spirits and cocktails.

Theory topics: wine areas and products; principal grapes and where grown; international wine laws (EC, US, Australia, others); fortified wines, vinification, storage and handling; distillation, spirits and liqueurs; beers and ciders and why styles vary; storing products in optimum condition.

MS Theory feedback: the goal is comprehension; four question types: simple short answer, extrapolation simple short answer, complex structure extrapolation simple short answer, and logical reasoning (short explanation of a concept).

MS Theory feedback groups topics into Cause & Effect (climate, geography, grape growing, grape variety, non-wine base material, law and production, soil, style, vintage climate and style, wine law, winemaking) and Tableside (classification and hierarchy, general and label terms, history and lore, producers and brands, named vineyards, price, vintage price and reputation).

The resource guide: the MS Diploma is a significant step up in difficulty from Advanced; the exam relies heavily on foundational knowledge from the Introductory, Certified and Advanced levels; master core principles rather than obscure details.

The resource guide: even the best books can be outdated on publication; balance them with current sources such as government regulation and marketing bodies, importer and producer websites, and educational platforms. With conflicting sources, rely on the most established, academic and contemporary.
Theory answer guidelines: sweetness, acidity, alcohol, body and tannin answers use Deductive Tasting Method terminology; volume, distance and other measurements use the units in the question.

Students must first pass Theory and then have three consecutive years to pass the remaining two parts; a student who passes one or two parts may retake the failed ones; if all three are not passed in three years the entire exam must be retaken.

Forced Wait Policy: a forced one-year wait for under 45% on the first attempt, under 55% on the second attempt in consecutive years, under 67% on the third attempt in consecutive years; candidates may sit each year while they keep 67% or higher (within 10% of the 75% needed). The policy is meant to give time to reassess and prepare.
A voluntary year off between attempts, or a forced wait, resets the percentage requirement clock.

The MS Theory feedback example recommends that any changes made before sitting Practical & Tasting that year be small; foundational shifts so close to the exam are likely to lower confidence and performance.

unverified: The window after a Theory pass: the Court's page says 'three consecutive years' and elsewhere 'two more attempts (one per calendar year)' after the first year. Both describe the same window; the lesson says three years, as the Court's page explains.

The one-hour length of the Theory, the 3 red and 3 white split of the tasting and the 5 to 10 year estimate appear only on the Court's About page, not on the exam page. They are stated with that attribution.
Pass rates, fees, dates, exam cities and the number of Master Sommeliers are left out on purpose. The feedback examples are templates with placeholder numbers.
The Court's illustrative theory questions and the example questions in the feedback report are not copied; the question-type list is described in our own words.

stops.name: Pass Advanced
stops.text: Those who pass the **Advanced** exam are eligible to apply. The Introductory, Certified and Advanced levels are the required steps before it.

stops.name: Apply with intent
stops.text: Candidates file an **Application of Intent**; an email saying you plan to sit is not accepted. First-timers file the **Theory** application. Anyone already holding Theory files the **Practical and Tasting** application.

stops.name: Meet the panel
stops.text: Every examiner is a Master Sommelier, chosen by the **Examination Committee** under the Court's examiner rotation policy.

read.mixup: The **Theory** application is for first-timers and anyone who has reset. The **Practical and Tasting** application is only for those holding at least Theory.

read.bigIdea: Same three parts as Advanced. A higher bar.
read.where: The diploma mirrors the Advanced exam: **theory**, a **practical** in wine service and business, and a **deductive tasting**. What changes is the depth and the mark: **75%** on each part, against 60% at Advanced. Come in working attire, with your own tools.

stops.name: Theory
stops.text: Spoken answers to a panel. The Court's About page describes a one-hour verbal exam that reaches past wine into beer, sake, spirits and cocktails.

stops.name: Practical
stops.text: Aperitifs, **glassware** for every beverage and room, wines with vintages for the menu, **decanting** when needed, spirits in proper **portions**, and **complaints** handled with diplomacy. Feedback covers a **Sparkling table**, a **Decanting table** and **Business of the Sommelier**.

stops.name: Tasting
stops.text: Six wines in **25 minutes**, described aloud: grape, country, district and appellation, and **vintage** where it applies. The About page says three whites and three reds.

read.mixup: **75%** is the Master Sommelier mark on each part. **60%** was the Advanced mark. A strong score on one part doesn't carry another.

read.bigIdea: Pass Theory, then the three-year clock starts.
read.where: The Court sets the order: **Theory** first. Passing it opens a **three-year window** for the **Practical** and the **Tasting**, as the Court's page explains. Miss the window and you retake everything.

stops.name: The window
stops.text: After Theory you have **three consecutive years** to pass the other two parts. Inside that window you retake only the part you failed.

stops.name: The forced wait
stops.text: A low Theory score means a **one-year wait**: below **45%** on a first try, **55%** on a second in a row, **67%** on a third in a row. The Court says the point is time to rethink and prepare.

stops.name: The reset
stops.text: Take a year off, by choice or by rule, and the **percentage clock resets**.

stops.name: Close to the exam
stops.text: The Court's feedback example advises only **small changes** before the Practical and Tasting. Big shifts late tend to cost confidence.

read.mixup: The **three-year window** starts after a Theory pass and covers Practical and Tasting. The **forced wait** follows a low Theory score: a year off before you sit Theory again.
